newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: FEATURE - Turkmen camel herders blaze trail to free market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Turkmen camel herders blaze trail to free market.

text.p: Five camels loped over a rise in the dunes, broken by grey-green desert scrub, slow and hot-legged under a strong sun.
Two boys followed on horseback. The grey walls of a dry canyon opened behind them in the empty wastes of Turkmenistan's Kara Kum, or Black Sands, desert.

The boys were taking the camels to sell in Kyzyl Arvat, a small market town about 250 km (150 miles) northwest of the capital Ashgabat, where they could expect to sell each for a million manat -- about $400 -- a lot of money in these parts.

Independence following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 for this desert republic of 3.8 million has breathed new life into camel herding and the proud Turkmens' traditional nomadic existence. It has also mapped out a tentative path to a market economy.
CAMEL HERDERS FREED OF SOVIET CONSTRAINTS
"My father taught me how to herd camels, he and my grandfather were herders," said 48-year-old Bazarklich Saparov.
Unshaven and wearing an old checked shirt, Saparov relishes the lack of government interference at Mele Koch, a small settlement of 20 families in the middle of trackless desert.
"In Soviet times you could only keep one camel and 10 sheep and you had to pay for each," Saparov recalled as two young falcons, to be raised for hunting, screeched angrily in a cage at his feet.
"Now it is better, you can have as many animals as you like, you can take the land for yourself and no one tells you how many camels or sheep you can breed."
Saparov took 10 camels, wearing dyed camel-hair amulets around their necks to ward off the evil eye, down to a nearby well to drink.
The creatures crowded together and put their long necks down to the well, looked guardedly out from under long eyelashes, grunted and sucked in water through their full, velvety lips.
HERDING SEES PRIVATISATION THROUGH BACK DOOR
While most land has not been privatised, the government is turning a blind eye to privately produced vegetables and livestock raised on state land.

It marks a quiet but important turning point in Turkmenistan, in many ways yet to wake from its Soviet era torpor, as strongman President Saparmurat Niyazov gently turns his back on a planned economy.
"They're abandoning state support but not announcing it," a western diplomat in Ashgabat explained.

The basis for the survival of the Turkmens' desert life -- for them as idyllic as an Englishman's country garden -- was noted by Gustav Krist, an Austrian soldier turned carpet merchant who travelled in disguise through Soviet Central Asia in the 1920s.

"Their highest law, the dab, is tradition and custom. They never deviate from it by a hair's breadth, so that the Turcoman of today lives exactly as his forefathers of a thousand years ago," Krist wrote.

He said that if the Soviet authorities tried to interfere :"they simply strike their tents and wander off to other places in the immeasurable wastes of the Black Sand, the Qara Qum, into which very few Europeans have as yet ventured".
TRADITIONS JEALOUSLY GUARDED
A few squat houses standing next to large round yurts, or tents, and television sets running off an ancient diesel generator are the only concessions to modernity at Mele Koch.

Ogylbebe Tuakeliyeva, wearing flower-print leggings, a cotton tunic and headscarf, much like Pakistan's shawal kameez, busied about her home, as if imitating the dung beatles which tirelessly rolled balls of camel manure across the sand outside.
After she slapped bread dough on the inside of a mud oven fired with saxaul, the ubiquitous scrubby bush of the Kara Kum, she wandered over to an enclosure of thorns to milk her camels.
Competing with the foal for the udders, Tuakeliyeva filled a zinc bucket with thick, sour-tasting milk.
She brought it back to her yurt and served it along with a bowl of salted mutton.
"My husband's family bought me for one camel," said Tuakeliyeva, who explained that "kalim", or dowry was still very much current in the desert.
"Familes expect camels, carpets and gold, it is all very expensive now," she said between slurps from a cracked cup of green tea.
TURKMEN WERE FAMED "MAN STEALERS"
Absent from inside the yurt were the arsenal of rifles, pistols, daggers and sabres that a Turkmen would have hung from the tent walls before the 1917 Russian revolution.

The Turkmens were the last Central Asian people to be subdued by tsarist troops as Russia expanded its empire. In a final battle in 1881, every Turkmen in the Geok Teppe fortress was killed or later massacred as they fled into the desert.

Russia was determined to teach the "man-stealing Turcomans", who once made a steady living out of slavery and plundering hapless caravans and Russian expeditions that dared cross the Kara Kum, a lesson they would not forget.
One Turkmen elder boasted to Krist that his tribe had captured and sold into slavery some 70,000 Persians. "He saw nothing in this worthy of comment, still less anything reprehensible," Krist wrote.
Saparaga Amanklichev, 84 and sporting a black sheepskin "telpek" at a rakish angle on his gaunt head, said proudly: "We're returning to our life before the revolution."
Darkness fell and the menfolk unrolled their bedding on raised wooden boards under the brilliant stars.

"Sleeping in the sands is ten times better than sleeping in the village," Amanklichev said wistfully of his time herding camels across the Kara Kum. "Especially in the spring when you can smell the flowers -- it is paradise, it is life."
